newsitem.title: GERMANY: BUNDESBANKER SAYS STILL EMU STILL POSSIBLE.
newsitem.headline: BUNDESBANKER SAYS STILL EMU STILL POSSIBLE.

text.p: European nations face hard work ahead to qualify for Europe's planned currency union, but the union can still begin on time if current plans are realised, a senior Bundesbank official said on Wednesday.

Although nations' progress on meeting the strict entry criteria for EMU been mixed to date, Bundesbank council member Hans-Juergen Koebnick said there was still hope for the Euro to be launched on January 1, 1999 with six to eight nations.

"Currently EU nations' budget plans still allow a possible meeting of the Treaty criteria in spirit and the letter," Koebnick told an audience at the inauguration of a savings bank on near the French-German border.

"That means the currency union begins on January 1, 1999, it will begin with six to eight nations including Germany and France," Koebnick, also president of the state central bank in the Rhineland Palatinate and Saar regions said.

But Koebnick also warned that EU nations' progress on meeting the entry criteria -- which require that budget deficits do not exceed three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) and that government debt does not exceed 60 percent of GDP -- was still not satisfactory or sufficient.
Both Germany, where Koebnick predicted the 1996 budget deficit would be around four percent of GDP, and France needed to step up spending cuts in order to meet the deadline.
"As measured against the criteria, convergence in fiscal policies in the European Union is currently still not sufficient," Koebnick said.

Pointing to the fact that Germany's budget deficit is likely to rise this year from last year's 3.5 percent level, Koebnick concluded, "Germany is moving in the wrong direction in terms of meeting the deficit criteria."
Turning to neighboring France, Koebnick warned, "the situation in France is similarly unsatisfactory, and France still needs to take significant steps to reach the three percent level in time."
European political leaders will in 1998 determine which nation's 1997 economic data qualify them for currency union.
On the other hand nations were making better progress in meeting requirements for low and stable prices across Europe.
Koebnick said there were a number of signs that German inflation, currently running at an annual rate of 1.4 percent, would remain stable after the currency union begins.
Even in Europe as a whole, "there are good chances that Europe will remain a zone with stable prices after the currency union begins," Koebnick said.

Looking ahead to the time when political leaders will determine which nations pass the entry test, Koebnick urged the criteria must be interpreted very strictly, warning a lax interpretation could jeopardise long-term stability.

Referring to the fact that Germany had failed to meet this target in recent years, Koebnick said, "whoever argues for a generous interpretation of the fiscal criteria calls into question the guiding lines and basic tenets of German fiscal policy over the last few decades."
While Koebnick said there was still a chance for currency union to go ahead on time, he also said discussion about a possible delay is not damaging to the entire undertaking.

"Whoever suggests a possible delay of the starting date for EMU, by a previously precisely defined time frame, does not tarnish the project's credibility but rather opens room to avoid deficits in credibility for the union to remain a stability oriented union," he said.
